title: Recognize the source before interpreting it

sourceWindow.context: This is the opening verse of the Torah, presented as a verse rather than a rabbinic case or discussion.

teachingMove: Before asking what a source means, name its family. Genre tells you what kinds of questions will help.
prompt: Which first move best orients you to this source?

choices.text: Identify it as a Torah verse, then notice its speaker, action, and setting.
Treat it as a final halakhic ruling and look immediately for a practical verdict.
Treat it as a Gemara debate and divide its words into challenge and response.

feedback.correct: Yes. Naming the source family gives you the right reading moves without asking you to know everything first.
feedback.incorrect: Start with genre: this is a Torah verse. Then ask verse-shaped questions about speaker, action, scene, and repeated language.

evidencePreview: I can recognize a Jewish source family before I interpret it.

title: Find the case before the ruling

sourceWindow.translation: From when may one recite Shema in the evenings?
sourceWindow.context: The Mishnah opens by defining a concrete case: the permitted time for evening Shema.

teachingMove: A Mishnah often becomes readable when you separate the situation being governed from the ruling about it.
prompt: What is the case this Mishnah asks you to locate?

choices.text: A person needs to know when the evening window for reciting Shema begins.
A person needs to decide who first composed every word of the prayer.
A person needs to reconstruct the political history of the Second Temple.

feedback.correct: Right. The case is the evening recitation window; the following positions define its boundary.
feedback.incorrect: Return to the opening question. The case is practical and bounded: when evening Shema may begin.

evidencePreview: I can identify the case a Mishnah is governing.
